title: EC75

agents.name: Epirubicin
agents.explanation: Epirubicin interferes with enzymes and DNA processes needed for cell division. It can also affect heart muscle, so the team considers previous exposure and cardiac risk.
agents.watch: Report pain or burning at the infusion site immediately. New breathlessness or chest symptoms need prompt review. Red urine for a short time can be a drug-colour effect; pain, clots or persistent bleeding still need advice.
risks: Low counts, infection and mouth ulcers
Severe tissue injury if the infusion leaks

agents.name: Cyclophosphamide
agents.explanation: Cyclophosphamide is activated in the body and damages DNA. This helps stop dividing cancer cells but can also affect blood-cell production and reproductive tissues.
agents.watch: Use the prescribed anti-sickness and hydration plan. Report fever, painful urination or blood in the urine.

purpose: Treatment to control cancer and symptoms, with regular review of benefit and side effects.
schedule_summary: Epirubicin and cyclophosphamide on Day 1 every 21 days while beneficial and tolerated, within the lifetime anthracycline limit.

phases_title: The phases and how they connect
phases_note: Review benefit, side effects and cumulative exposure; the NCCP source does not set a universal four- or six-cycle course.
timeline_note: These broad symptom bands are educational possibilities, not measured risk curves. Infusion days are the planned schedule; delays require a new clinical plan.
safety_note: Fever, shivers, sudden illness, severe breathing changes or chest pain need prompt assessment on any day.
teachback: Can you explain which medicines you are receiving now? What symptoms mean you should call urgently? Which blood tests, scans or heart checks come next, and who arranges them?
consent_support: Use this information to discuss the treatment goal, alternatives, phase changes, important risks and monitoring with your team. It supports the approved local consent process.
urgent_extra: Seek prompt advice for fever, shivering, severe diarrhoea, painful mouth ulcers, inability to drink, new chest symptoms or a painful/leaking line. Do not wait for the next cycle.

support.title: A clear anti-sickness plan
support.text: Take the prescribed prevention medicines and keep the rescue instructions. Contact the team if nausea or vomiting prevents drinking.

support.title: Infection and growth-factor plan
support.text: The team decides whether growth-factor injections are needed and gives the exact days. Fever or suddenly feeling unwell needs immediate advice.

support.title: Hydration and urinary symptoms
support.text: Agree fluid intake with your team, especially if you have a heart or kidney fluid restriction. Report painful urination or blood in the urine.

support.title: Before treatment
support.text: Discuss fertility, contraception, other medicines and line access. Tell staff immediately about burning or pain at the infusion site.

questions.q: Why might this treatment be selected for me?
questions.a: EC75 may be selected to control metastatic breast cancer when chemotherapy is appropriate. Hormone receptors, HER2 status, symptoms, speed of cancer growth, previous medicines and heart health guide the choice. Some people have endocrine or targeted options that better fit their cancer.

questions.q: Who arranges the scans and tests?
questions.a: Your treating service should book the planned checks, review the results and explain any change. If an expected appointment is missing, contact the team; this map does not book tests or confirm that they have happened.

chapters.title: Why this treatment?
chapters.intro: EC75 may be selected to control metastatic breast cancer when chemotherapy is appropriate. Hormone receptors, HER2 status, symptoms, speed of cancer growth, previous medicines and heart health guide the choice. Some people have endocrine or targeted options that better fit their cancer.

items.title: The sequence
items.text: Epirubicin and cyclophosphamide on Day 1 every 21 days while beneficial and tolerated, within the lifetime anthracycline limit.

items.title: Alternatives and your priorities
items.text: Ask what alternatives fit your cancer, what the treatment aims to achieve, and how its practical demands fit your life. The team can discuss personal benefits and risks.

chapters.title: Checks across treatment
chapters.intro: Your team arranges, reviews and acts on tests; an overdue result needs follow-up.

items.title: Blood tests
items.text: Baseline FBC, kidney and liver tests; repeat before each chemotherapy cycle.

items.title: Heart monitoring
items.text: ESC supplementary guidance: baseline echo before anthracycline treatment. High/very-high cardiac risk: echo every two anthracycline cycles (for example before cycles 3 and 5 when continuing), and within 3 months after completion. All adults: echo within 12 months after completion. Other repeat tests depend on risk, cumulative exposure and symptoms.

items.title: ECG
items.text: Baseline ECG in the NCCP anthracycline source; repeat for symptoms or clinical risk. An ECG does not replace an echo.

items.title: Cancer scans
items.text: Record disease sites before treatment. Response imaging is generally considered every 2–4 months under ESMO guidance, adjusted to symptoms and disease pace. For a 21-day course this is approximately after 3–6 cycles; the team chooses the scan and exact checkpoint. New symptoms may need earlier assessment.

chapters.title: Surgery, radiotherapy and later treatment
chapters.intro: In metastatic disease, surgery and radiotherapy are individual decisions for symptoms or selected local-control needs; they are not automatic steps after every course.

items.title: Hormone-receptor-positive disease
items.text: Endocrine treatment is considered when appropriate for the cancer biology and setting. It has its own schedule and monitoring; it is not automatically part of this chemotherapy prescription.

items.title: Bone health
items.text: DEXA is linked to an aromatase inhibitor, ovarian suppression, treatment-induced menopause or other bone risk—not automatically to every chemotherapy course. The endocrine team confirms baseline testing and risk-based repeat scans.

items.title: Markers and follow-up
items.text: Tumour markers can support selected metastatic assessments but must not alone determine progression or treatment changes.

steps.title: Before the first visit
steps.text: Blood tests, relevant cardiac assessment, medicines review, fertility discussion and the consent conversation come first.

steps.title: Plan venous access
steps.text: A cannula, PICC or implanted port may be used. If a port is chosen, a trained team inserts it in a separate procedure with local anaesthetic and sometimes sedation; the team explains fasting, blood-thinner and wound instructions.

steps.title: Infusion day
steps.text: Staff check the line, give prescribed premedicines and treatment, and observe for reactions. Tell them immediately about burning, pain, rash or breathlessness.

steps.title: Home and next review
steps.text: This regimen does not routinely need a take-home infusion pump. Staff disconnect the infusion; a port is de-accessed when appropriate. Keep line-care and next-visit instructions.

details.title: Port insertion and removal
details.text: The line team explains placement, dressing care and when normal activities can resume. A port is accessed with a special needle during treatment. Removal of the implanted device is a separate planned procedure when no longer needed; do not remove or adjust it yourself.

details.title: PICC care and urgent line symptoms
details.text: A PICC usually needs regular dressing and flushing appointments even between treatments. Fever, redness, swelling, pain, leakage or damage requires prompt advice. Your hospital supplies the exact care instructions.

details.title: Visit time and transport
details.text: Allow time for blood review, preparation, treatment and observation. Your unit confirms the full visit duration. Arrange transport or an escort where advised.

details.title: Phase-specific visit pattern
details.text: These medicines are given on Day 1 in the unit. No take-home infusion pump is part of this regimen; port needle removal after a visit is different from removal of the implanted port.
